headline: Apple's CEO Says Good Products Matter More Than Just Using AI

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: John Ternus is the boss of Apple, a big company that makes phones and computers. People have said Apple is slow at using AI, which is computer technology that can think and learn like a helper. Apple waited a long time to make its voice helper, called Siri, smarter. It finally came out this past summer. In an interview, Ternus said he feels good about how Apple is doing. He explained that Apple will use AI in its products, but only when it truly helps people. He does not want Apple to add AI just so they can say they have it. He said the most important thing is making something people really enjoy using, whether or not AI is involved. Someone also asked if AI could change things so much that people might not need apps anymore. Ternus said that could be easier, but he believes making products is something humans love doing by hand and heart. This shows Apple wants to be careful and thoughtful about new technology instead of rushing to use it everywhere.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, spoke in an interview about how his company is handling artificial intelligence, or AI, which is technology that can act smart, like understanding language or making decisions. For the past couple of years, people have said Apple is behind other tech companies when it comes to AI. One example is that Apple delayed releasing a smarter version of Siri, its voice assistant, and it did not come out until this summer. Even with that criticism, Ternus said he feels confident about where Apple stands. He explained that Apple definitely plans to use AI in future products, but not just for the sake of having it. He believes AI should work quietly in the background, so people don't even notice whether AI or regular software made something happen. What matters most to him is whether people actually enjoy using the product. The interviewer also asked if AI could change things so much that apps might not even be needed anymore, since AI programs called 'agents' could do tasks on their own. Ternus responded that while that might be convenient, he thinks creating products is a very human and personal process that Apple cares about. This story matters because it shows how a major tech company is thinking carefully about balancing new technology with what actually makes customers happy, instead of just following trends.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Apple's CEO, John Ternus, addressed criticism that his company has fallen behind in the artificial intelligence race during a recent interview with journalist Steven Levy. Artificial intelligence, or AI, refers to computer systems that can perform tasks that normally require human thinking, like understanding speech or making predictions. Over the past couple of years, many people have pointed out that Apple seemed slower than competitors like Google or Microsoft to roll out powerful AI features. One major example is Siri, Apple's voice assistant, which was supposed to get a major AI upgrade but was delayed multiple times before finally launching this past summer. Despite this criticism, Ternus, who became CEO in September, said he feels good about Apple's current approach. He explained that Apple will continue to use AI in its products, but he does not believe in adding AI just to say the company has it. Instead, he wants AI to work so smoothly that customers don't even think about whether a feature was powered by AI or traditional software. For Ternus, the real measure of success is whether people genuinely love using the product, not whether it includes the latest technology trend. The interviewer pushed further, asking whether AI could transform Apple's entire business model, since AI 'agents' — programs that can complete tasks independently — might someday make apps unnecessary altogether. Ternus acknowledged that this could make life more convenient, but he emphasized that creating products is a deeply human and personal process that Apple values deeply. This conversation is important because it reveals how one of the world's largest tech companies is thinking about the pressure to adopt AI quickly. Many companies rush to add AI features to stay competitive, but Ternus's comments suggest Apple is trying to prioritize thoughtful design and user satisfaction over simply keeping up with trends. This debate affects everyday technology users because it influences what kinds of features show up in future iPhones, computers, and other devices people use daily.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: In a recent interview with Wired journalist Steven Levy, Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, pushed back against the narrative that his company has lagged behind in the artificial intelligence industry. Artificial intelligence, or AI, describes computer systems designed to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as understanding natural language, recognizing patterns, or making decisions. Apple has faced scrutiny over the past couple of years for seemingly moving slower than rivals in adopting AI technology. This criticism intensified after Apple delayed a more advanced version of Siri, its voice assistant, which didn't launch until this past summer despite earlier expectations. Ternus, a longtime Apple executive who officially took over as CEO at the start of September, acknowledged that opinions about Apple's AI strategy vary widely, but he firmly stated that he feels confident in the company's current direction. According to Ternus, Apple intends to continue integrating AI into its products, but not simply for the sake of appearing innovative or keeping pace with competitors. He explained that when AI is implemented correctly, users shouldn't have to distinguish between AI-powered features and traditional software; the technology should work seamlessly in the background. For Ternus, the ultimate goal isn't whether AI was involved in building something, but whether the final product genuinely resonates with and is loved by its users. Levy also challenged Ternus on a bigger question: could AI fundamentally disrupt Apple's ecosystem, particularly through the rise of AI 'agents' — programs capable of independently completing tasks — potentially making traditional apps obsolete? Ternus responded that while such a shift could simplify life, he views the creation of products as a deeply human and personal endeavor, one that Apple is passionate about preserving. This exchange highlights a broader tension within the tech industry: the pressure to rapidly adopt flashy new technology versus the discipline of prioritizing thoughtful, user-focused design. Many companies feel compelled to showcase AI capabilities to remain competitive and relevant in a fast-moving market, sometimes at the expense of genuinely useful or polished products. Ternus's comments suggest that Apple is intentionally resisting this pressure, betting that careful, deliberate integration of AI will serve customers better in the long run than rushing out features just to keep up appearances. This philosophy could shape the future of products millions of people rely on daily, from smartphones to computers, and it reflects an ongoing debate about what truly makes technology valuable, innovation for its own sake or meaningful improvement to everyday life.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Apple CEO John Ternus recently defended the company's measured approach to artificial intelligence during an interview with Wired's Steven Levy, pushing back against persistent criticism that Apple has fallen behind competitors in the AI race. Artificial intelligence, broadly defined as computer systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human cognition, such as language processing, pattern recognition, and decision-making, has become a central battleground in the tech industry, with companies racing to integrate increasingly sophisticated AI features into their products. Apple has faced particular scrutiny on this front, especially after delaying the rollout of a significantly upgraded version of Siri, its voice assistant, which didn't launch until this past summer, well behind initial expectations and years after competitors introduced comparable AI-driven assistants. Ternus, a longtime Apple executive who assumed the CEO role at the beginning of September, acknowledged that public opinion on Apple's AI strategy is divided, but he expressed clear confidence in the company's current trajectory, stating simply that he likes where Apple stands. Rather than framing AI adoption as a race to be won, Ternus articulated a philosophy centered on seamless integration and user experience. He explained that Apple plans to continue leveraging AI in its product lineup, but emphasized that the company is not interested in deploying AI merely to project an image of technological relevance. Instead, he suggested that successful AI implementation should be invisible to the end user, meaning people shouldn't need to consciously register whether a given feature was powered by AI or conventional software engineering. The true benchmark, in his view, is whether the resulting product earns genuine affection and usefulness from its customers, a metric that prioritizes outcome over method. The conversation took a more speculative turn when Levy pressed Ternus on whether AI could fundamentally reshape Apple's broader ecosystem, particularly through the emergence of autonomous AI agents, software capable of independently executing complex tasks, potentially rendering traditional applications and even app stores obsolete. Ternus's response was notably measured; he conceded that such a transformation could offer significant convenience, but he firmly maintained that the process of creating products remains an inherently human and personal craft, one that Apple remains deeply committed to preserving rather than fully automating. This exchange encapsulates a significant tension within the broader technology sector: the competitive pressure to rapidly showcase cutting-edge AI capabilities versus the discipline required to build genuinely polished, user-centered products. Many companies have faced criticism for prioritizing flashy AI announcements over substantive improvements, sometimes releasing half-finished features to satisfy market expectations and investor pressure. Ternus's comments position Apple as deliberately resistant to this trend, suggesting a strategic bet that thoughtful, restrained AI integration will ultimately serve both the company's reputation and its customers better than a rush to match competitors feature-for-feature. Given Apple's massive global user base and influence over consumer technology trends, this philosophy could have lasting implications for how AI is woven into everyday devices, potentially setting a precedent that values deliberate craftsmanship over the industry's broader momentum toward rapid, sometimes indiscriminate AI deployment.

questions: Do you think technology companies should wait until a feature is really good before releasing it, even if that means falling behind competitors? Why or why not?
If AI assistants could someday do everything apps do now, how might that change the way you use your phone or computer at school or at home?
Apple's CEO says creating products should stay a 'human and personal' process. Why do you think some people might still want humans involved in making things, even when AI could do the job?
